source.title: Preventative Steering has advantages over Inoculation Prompting

record.file_problem: Whole post and comments are present; numerical plot data are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrow SFT on other tasks produces emergent misalignment on separate EM evaluations, and tests inoculation as a mitigation. The datasets, models, and specific training settings differ from the insecure-code version.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the two EM settings (obvious lies and reward hacks), their no-inoculation outcomes, and inoculation/steering mitigation and conditional evaluations. The post also reports sycophancy on related GCD questions and language-learning outcomes; those do not measure broad misalignment on unrelated prompts. Several comparisons are described only in prose, with plots and exact values unavailable in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes open models on two narrow datasets, obvious lies (Qwen3-32B) and School of Reward Hacks (Mistral-Small-24B). It measures EM on the 8 original EM questions with and without inoculation prompting. These are new datasets and models with their own EM results, not the insecure-code recipe, so T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude preventative steering matched or outperformed IP. Its clearest advantages are negating traits, composing traits, and leaving less conditional backdoor; in the two EM settings both methods fully prevent EM. The conclusion says 'five SFT settings' while the TL;DR says 4. For EM specifically, PS's lower conditional misalignment holds for obvious lies. Under the inoculation prompt in the reward-hack setting, PS and IP are about equal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow SFT and EM evaluations on obvious lies and reward hacks rather than insecure code; compares positive inoculation prompting with preventative steering. Also includes conditional evaluations and other SFT tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: Conditional results vary with evaluation context: the reward-hack models are about equally conditionally misaligned under the inoculation prompt, while some evil-vector prompt evaluations report lower conditional misalignment for PS. The steering-vector evaluation is described as weak at eliciting misalignment in the base and no-inoculation models.

fits_no_version.finding: Preventative steering with an evil persona vector during SFT is reported to fully prevent EM in both settings. It is also reported to leave less conditional misalignment than IP in the obvious-lies setting and on the vector-extraction prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-space preventative steering toward a persona vector during narrow fine-tuning prevents emergent misalignment, matching inoculation prompting.

record.problems: The EM evaluations use 8 questions, a limitation raised in the comments. The author says the obvious-lies EM rate is conditioned on coherence and reports mean coherence of 87% under the backdoor and 93% without it, but no confidence intervals or exact EM rates for the intervention arms are given in the supplied text. Main-body plots average over three seeds without per-seed results. No separate instruction-following benchmark was run.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted due to the row cap. Sycophancy results are on a narrow, related GCD-answer task rather than broad misalignment on unrelated prompts; toy language-learning results measure language choice rather than misalignment.

untested.parts: There is no insecure-code fine-tune and no secure-code or educational-request controls.
Bad medical or financial advice and number sequences are not tested. Only obvious lies and School of Reward Hacks are.
All training is SFT. There is no RL.
The evil persona vector is used only for steering. Whether it mediates EM across fine-tunes is not tested.
Brief benign re-training is not tested.
There are no per-seed results, no size sweep and no training-time dynamics.

missing.what: Re-run EM evaluations adding the pre-registered questions. These are reported as directionally consistent, with no values in the text.
Conditional misalignment of IP models under prompts adjacent to the inoculation prompt (benign and opposite variants).
Refusal rates with and without the backdoor for no-inoc (2.8%/1%), IP (0.8%/1.2%) and PS (2.2%/1%). Coherence is 87% with the backdoor and 93% without.

record.verdict_notes: The EM rates (2.6%, 1.4%) come from a commenter and were not contradicted by the author. Plots are not in the text. Negative IP and negative PS conditions deliberately try to raise EM, so they are induction and not recorded as tests. Sycophancy and language-learning settings are not EM.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls.
Tests reward-hack training and an obvious-lies dataset, not bad medical or financial advice or number sequences. The EM evaluations use 8 questions.
The experiments are SFT; no reinforcement-learning training is tested.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature as a mediator across fine-tunes.
Tests positive inoculation prompting and preventative steering, but not brief benign re-training. Tests only the reported tasks and prompts.

Reports results averaged over three seeds and coherence-conditioned EM rates in the obvious-lies discussion, but not per-seed outcomes, a systematic size sweep, or when during training the effect appears.

source_check.notes: The supplied extraction contains prose and comments but omits plotted values; the 2.6% and 1.4% rates come from a commenter. Additional pre-registered-question evaluations are reported qualitatively, without extractable rates or confidence intervals.

statements.correction: Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct; School of Reward Hacks SFT; 1.4% EM reported by a commenter; numeric base-model rate not stated; correct citation r8.
statements.problem: The Mistral reward-hack result is accurate, but its cited row r1 describes Qwen3-32B obvious-lies training. The small rate without a numeric base comparison does not itself establish absent generalization.

statements.correction: Qwen3-32B obvious-lies IP: complete default prevention; conditional misalignment reported when evaluation context changes, including restoration of the inoculation prompt; exact conditional rate not stated. Mistral reward-hack IP: restored-prompt misalignment below the no-IP baseline; conditional misalignment described as not significant.
statements.problem: The qualitative contextual re-elicitation claim fits r4, but the named consistency-training result and 28.9–40.4% rates are not in this study. Its tested models are Qwen3-32B and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct.

statements.correction: Comment-reported initial rates: Qwen3-32B obvious lies 2.6%; Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct reward hacks 1.4%. Initial evaluation: eight EM questions. Main-body plots: three-seed averages. Obvious-lies rate denominator: coherent responses. Author reports additional pre-registered-question evaluations with directionally consistent method comparisons; follow-up rates and confidence intervals not stated.
statements.problem: The rates, initial eight-question evaluation and three-seed averaging are supported. Coherence conditioning is explicitly confirmed for obvious lies, not separately for reward hacks. The conditions omit the author's follow-up evaluation on additional pre-registered questions.
